summary: This informational memo clarifies how the 32-bit IPv4 address space is interpreted in practice, since its meaning has changed a great deal since it was first defined. It describes the situation as it stood rather than defining a new standard.

plainLanguage.summary: An IPv4 address used to be both a name for a computer and its address on the network, and it never changed. Neither is true any more. This memo explains what an IPv4 address means today, and what breaks when it is used for both jobs at once.

questions: how is ipv4 address space used today
what is the difference between an ip address identifier and locator
how do nats change ipv4 addresses
why do ipv4 addresses not stay unique
subtitle: What an IPv4 address means now that the same number can be reused and can stop being valid.

tldr.problem: An IPv4 address was designed to do two jobs at once, and the way the Internet has grown has made the two jobs pull apart.
tldr.mechanism: The memo separates an address used as an identifier, which names the other end of a session, from one used as a locator, which says where a packet has to go, and then lists what has broken: private address space, address translation, renumbering, multicast and anycast.
tldr.outcome: An address is still a good locator, so delivery still works, but it is no longer a reliable identifier, which puts end-to-end security and session state built on the address in question.

facts.label: Identifier uniqueness
facts.value: Unique within each set of inter-communicating hosts

today: RFC 2101 is an Informational memo from February 1997, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the state of IPv4 addressing at that time and is a snapshot rather than a specification, and its Security Considerations section points back to its own sections 4.1 and 5 rather than adding separate material.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The main purpose of this note is to clarify the current interpretation of the 32-bit IP version 4 address space, whose significance has changed substantially since it was originally defined in 1981. The clarification is intended to assist protocol designers, product implementors, Internet service providers and user sites. It aims to avoid misunderstandings about IP addresses that can result from the substantial changes that have taken place in the last few years, as a result of the Internet's exponential growth.

A short section on IPv6 addresses mentions the main points of similarity with, and difference from, IPv4. The memo is the work of the Internet Architecture Board, and its Security Considerations section points back to two of its own sections rather than adding new material.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is a description of the world as it was in early 1997, not a proposal to change anything. Its value is in naming two jobs that had been done by one field.

sections.title: Terminology: Identifier and Locator
sections.content:
It is well understood that in computer networks the concepts of directories, names, network addresses and routes are separate and must be analysed separately. It is also necessary to sub-divide the concept of network address into at least two notions, identifier and locator, which was perhaps less well understood when RFC 791 was written. In this document a host is any system originating or terminating IPv4 packets, and a router is any system forwarding IPv4 packets from one host or router to another.

An identifier is a bit string used throughout the lifetime of a communication session between two hosts, to identify one of the hosts as far as the other is concerned. Such an identifier is used to verify the source of incoming packets as being truly the other end of the communication concerned, for example in the TCP pseudo-header or in an IP Security association, and traditionally the source IPv4 address in every packet is used for this. A locator is a bit string used to identify where a particular packet must be delivered, that is, it serves to locate the place in the Internet topology where the destination host is attached, and traditionally the destination IPv4 address in every packet is used for this. IP routing protocols interpret IPv4 addresses as locators and construct routing tables based on which routers claim to know a route towards the locators of particular hosts.

Both have requirements of uniqueness, and the requirements are different. Identifiers must be unique with respect to each set of inter-communicating hosts. Locators must be unique with respect to each set of inter-communicating routers, a routing realm. While locators must be unique within a given routing realm, that uniqueness could extend to more than one realm, so a set of realms with unique locators can be told apart from a set of realms with overlapping locators. Both also have requirements of lifetime, and those differ too: identifiers must be valid for at least the maximum lifetime of a communication between two hosts, while locators must be valid only as long as the routing mechanisms require, which could be shorter or longer than the lifetime of a communication.

It is a contingent fact of history that the same address space and the same fields in the IP header are used by RFC 791 and RFC 793 for both identifiers and locators, and that in the traditional Internet a host's identifier is identical to its locator, as well as being spatially unique and temporally unique. The ideal properties are easy to state: identifiers should be assigned at birth, never change and never be re-used, while locators should describe the host's position in the network's topology and should change whenever the topology changes. Unfortunately, neither of these ideals is met by IPv4 addresses, and the rest of the document is a snapshot of the real situation.
sections.plainLanguage: One field, two jobs. The source address names the other end of the conversation; the destination address says where to deliver the packet. The memo argues these should be separate things.

sections.title: Addresses Are No Longer Globally Unique Locators
sections.content:
RFC 1918 shows how corporate networks, that is intranets, may if necessary legitimately re-use a subset of the IPv4 address space, forming multiple routing realms, and at the boundary between two or more routing realms there is a spectrum of devices that enables communication between them.

At one end of the spectrum is a pure Application Layer Gateway (ALG), a device that acts as a termination point for the application layer data stream and is visible to the end user. With a non-transparent ALG, a user in realm A who wants to reach a user in realm B must first explicitly establish communication with the ALG, and only through it reach the other user. With a transparent ALG the connectivity is established transparently, so the user sees only connectivity to the other user. Both kinds of ALG must understand the syntax and semantics of the application data stream, and they are simple from the viewpoint of network layer architecture, since they appear as Internet hosts in each realm, acting as origination and termination points for communication. It is not necessarily the case that communicating via an ALG involves changes to the network header: an ALG could be used only at the beginning of a session for authentication, after which it goes away and communication continues natively.

At the other end of the spectrum is a Network Address Translator (NAT), a device that just modifies the network and the transport layer headers but does not understand the syntax and semantics of the application layer data stream. In the standard case of a NAT between a corporate network using private addresses and the public Internet, the NAT changes the source IPv4 address in packets going towards the Internet, and the destination IPv4 address in packets coming from the Internet. When a NAT interconnects routing realms with overlapping addresses, such as a direct connection between two intranets, it may modify both addresses. Because it modifies addresses in the IP header, the NAT also has to modify the transport, for example TCP or UDP, pseudo-header checksum.

The two kinds of device have their own limits. A NAT cannot support applications that carry IP addresses at the application layer, such as FTP with the PORT or PASV command, but it can support any application that does not do so. An ALG can support only the applications coded into it. Combining NAT and ALG functionality in one device can overcome some of the limits but not all: it would use the NAT functionality for the applications that do not carry IP addresses and the ALG functionality for those that do, and it would fail completely on an application that carries IP addresses when the device handles it with NAT rather than ALG functionality.

Two further consequences follow. Because both ALGs and NATs change the network header and the transport header, and because IP Security authentication headers assume that the addresses in the network header are preserved end-to-end, it is not clear how IP Security based authentication could be supported between a pair of hosts communicating through either one. Both are likely to force a boundary between two distinct IP Security domains, for authentication and for confidentiality, unless specific enhancements to IP Security are designed for the purpose. And interconnecting realms through ALGs or NATs relies on DNS: fully qualified domain names would need to be unique across the set of realms even where network layer addresses are not, but a site running a NAT or ALG probably needs two DNS servers, one inside and one outside, giving different answers to identical queries, and DNS security and some dynamic DNS updates will presumably not be valid across a NAT or ALG boundary. To summarize, since RFC 1918, the spatial uniqueness of an address has not really changed so much as been recognized as existing in multiple spaces, and the temporal uniqueness of an address is unchanged by RFC 1918.
sections.plainLanguage: Two organizations can now both use the same private addresses, and a device at the boundary rewrites them on the way out. Two devices do this job in different ways, and the memo compares what each one can and cannot carry.

sections.title: Addresses Are No Longer All Temporally Unique
sections.content:
As soon as address significance changes anywhere in the address space, it has in some sense changed everywhere, and this has already happened. IPv4 address blocks were for many years assigned chronologically, effectively at random with respect to network topology, which led to constantly growing routing tables, and that does not scale. Today hierarchical routing, CIDR, is used as a mechanism to improve scaling of routing within a routing realm, and especially within the Internet.

The scaling of CIDR is based on the assumption that address allocation reflects network topology as much as possible, and that boundaries for aggregation of addressing information need not be contained within a single organization, since they may span a provider and its subscribers. So if a subscriber changes its provider, then to avoid injecting additional overhead into the Internet routing system, the subscriber may need to renumber. Changing providers is only one possible reason for renumbering: RFC 1900 shows why renumbering is an increasingly frequent event, and both DHCP and PPP promote the use of dynamic address allocation. To summarize, since the development and deployment of DHCP and PPP, and since renumbering is likely to become a common event, IP address significance has indeed been changed. Spatial uniqueness should be the same, so addresses are still effective locators, but temporal uniqueness is no longer assured, and it may be quite short, possibly shorter than a TCP connection time. In such cases an IP address is no longer a good identifier, which has some impact on end-to-end security and breaks TCP in its current form.

The annex of the memo traces how this came about. IP address structure and IP routing were first designed around network number classes, the Class A, B and C networks. The growth of the Internet in the early 90s demanded improvements in both the scalability of the routing system and in the utilization of the address space, and the classful structure turned out to be inadequate, so during 1992 and 1993 the Internet adopted Classless Inter-Domain Routing. CIDR improves scalability by extending hierarchical routing beyond the level of individual subnets and networks, so that routing information can be aggregated at the level of sites and at the level of Internet service providers, letting an organization act as an aggregator for all the destinations within it and a provider act as an aggregator for all the destinations within its subscribers. It improves address space utilization by eliminating the notion of network classes and replacing it with contiguous variable size, power of 2, address blocks, which gives a better match between the amount of address space requested and the amount allocated. To benefit from this, CIDR introduces an inter-domain routing protocol, BGP-4, that provides aggregation at the level of sites and providers.

CIDR does not require every site that changes provider to renumber, but if none of them renumber, the Internet routing system might collapse under the routing information it would have to handle. Maintaining aggregator based allocation, to promote scalable routing, and supporting the ability of sites to change providers, to promote competition, both demand practical solutions for renumbering sites, and the need to contain the overhead of a rapidly growing routing system is likely to make renumbering more and more common. The need to scale the routing system, and the use of CIDR as the primary mechanism for scaling, has also produced the address lending policy as an alternative to the address ownership policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses now change hands more often. A company that switches internet provider may have to renumber, and a computer that connects by DHCP may get a different address each time. An address that changes mid-conversation can no longer be trusted to name the other end.

sections.title: Multicast, Anycast and the Summary
sections.content:
Since multicast was deployed, the debate over the meaning of IP addresses has to be separated into the meaning of source addresses and the meaning of destination addresses. A destination multicast address, a locator for a topologically spread group of hosts, can traverse a NAT, and is not necessarily restricted to an intranet or to the public Internet. Its lifetime can be short too.

An anycast address is an address that semantically locates any of a group of systems performing equivalent functions. There is no way such an address can be anything but a locator, and it can never serve as an identifier as defined in the memo, since it does not uniquely identify a host. In this case the effective temporal uniqueness, or useful lifetime, of an IP address can be less than the time taken to establish a TCP connection. TCP is used here simply to illustrate the idea of an association: many UDP based applications, or other systems layered on IP, allocate state after receiving or sending a first packet, based on the source and destination. All are affected by the absence of temporal uniqueness, whereas only the routing infrastructure is affected by changes in spatial uniqueness.

The memo's summary is that, due to dynamic address allocation and increasingly frequent network renumbering, the temporal uniqueness of IPv4 addresses is no longer globally guaranteed, which puts their use as identifiers into severe question. Due to the proliferation of intranets, spatial uniqueness is also no longer guaranteed across routing realms, and interconnecting routing realms could be accomplished via either ALGs or NATs. In principle such interconnection will have less functionality than if those intranets were directly connected, though in practice the difference in functionality may or may not matter, depending on individual circumstances.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of address can never name a single host: one that means a group of hosts, and one that means any of several machines doing the same job. They work as delivery addresses and nothing more.

sections.title: IPv6 Considerations
sections.content:
As far as temporal uniqueness is concerned, the IPv6 model is very similar to the current state of the IPv4 model, only more so. IPv6 will provide mechanisms to autoconfigure IPv6 addresses on IPv6 hosts, and prefix changes, requiring the global IPv6 addresses of all hosts under a given prefix to change, are to be expected. IPv6 will therefore amplify the existing problem of finding stable identifiers to be used for end-to-end security and for session bindings such as TCP state. The IAB feels that this is unfortunate, and that the transition to IPv6 would be an ideal occasion to provide upper layer end-to-end protocols with temporally unique identifiers. The exact nature of these identifiers requires further study.

As far as spatial uniqueness is concerned, the IPv6 address space is so big that a shortage of addresses, requiring an RFC 1918-like approach and address translation, is hardly conceivable. Although there is no shortage of IPv6 addresses, there is also a well-defined mechanism for obtaining link-local and site-local addresses. These properties of IPv6 do not prevent separate routing realms for IPv6, if that is desired, which would result in multiple security domains as well. While at the present moment the memo cannot identify a case in which multiple IPv6 routing realms would be required, it is also hard to give a definitive answer to whether there will be only one, or more than one. If there were more than one, such realms could be interconnected together via ALGs and NATs, and the considerations for those ALGs and NATs appear to be identical to those for IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 does not solve the problem of naming a host. It makes it worse, because addresses there are expected to change too, and it makes room for many more of them to be in use at once.

viz.caption: THE TWO JOBS ONE ADDRESS FIELD WAS ASKED TO DO

left.title: Identifier
left.desc: Names the other end of a session and must stay valid for as long as the session lasts.

right.title: Locator
right.desc: Says where the packet has to go, and changes whenever the topology changes.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO JOIN TWO ROUTING REALMS

cells: Any that do not carry IP addresses at the application layer

viz.caption: WHAT THE LOSS OF UNIQUENESS BREAKS

items.title: Spatial uniqueness
items.text: The same address can be used in another routing realm, so it does not identify one host across the Internet.

items.title: Temporal uniqueness
items.text: An address can be handed out again so quickly that it is no longer valid for the life of a session.

items.title: End-to-end security
items.text: IP Security authentication assumes the addresses are preserved, which a NAT or an ALG does not do.

items.title: Session state
items.text: TCP and UDP keep state keyed on addresses, which breaks when the address changes.

items.title: Renumbering
items.text: A site that changes provider may have to renumber, so its addresses change underneath it.

items.title: Multicast and anycast
items.text: Neither can serve as an identifier, and an anycast address can be shorter lived than a connection.
